analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federally funded construction to pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The Davis-Bacon Repeal Act, with 70 Republican cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Davis-Bacon Act, which requires contractors on federally financed construction projects to pay workers the wage that prevails locally for their trade. Repeal would let those contractors pay whatever lower wages they choose on federal jobs. It would also wipe out prevailing-wage requirements written into other laws. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and was never brought to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Contractors on federal construction projects benefit most: they could bid for federal work while paying below-prevailing wages, cutting labor costs. Open-shop (nonunion) builders, who already pay less than union-scale rates, would gain a competitive edge on federal contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction be paid the locally prevailing wage for their trade and class of work.
Declares that any reference in any other law to a Davis-Bacon wage requirement becomes null and void, erasing the wage floor from programs that rely on it.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects pay, through lower wages. Union-scale and other workers whose pay standards are benchmarked to prevailing rates would lose the leverage the federal wage floor provides. Taxpayers could see somewhat cheaper federal construction, but at the cost of wage standards for the workforce that builds it.

drawbacks.text: The repeal removes the only federal wage floor on publicly financed construction: the government would keep paying contractors for buildings and public works while the law stops requiring that the workers on those jobs earn the local going rate.

Because any reference to Davis-Bacon wage requirements in other statutes would be null and void, the repeal would strip wage protections well beyond the original Act itself, affecting any program that relied on them.

Supporters of repeal argued the prevailing-wage rules raise the cost of federally financed construction and disadvantage open-shop contractors; the savings, however, come primarily out of construction workers' paychecks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main measurable benefit is lower bids on federal construction, achieved by lowering wages on those jobs rather than by any efficiency gain. The cost falls on a specific, modest-paid workforce doing public work, and the bill's nullification clause would spread the cut to other laws' wage requirements. On balance, this is a wage cut for federal construction workers and a cost reduction for their employers, not a general public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee: after being referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, it was sent to a subcommittee and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on February 16, 2011, joined by Rep. Connie Mack, to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act.
Seventy House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on March 4, 2011.
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached the House floor and expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects kept their prevailing-wage protections, which they would have lost under this bill. Federal contractors who wanted to bid for federal work at below-prevailing wages did not get the change they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers kept their wage floor

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors bid for federally financed construction while paying below-prevailing wages, cutting their labor costs directly out of their workers' pay. The public would pay the same contractors for the same buildings with weaker wage standards attached.

Davis-Bacon sets the pay floor on federal jobs and supports union-scale rates; repeal would remove that protection from every federally financed project and, through the nullification clause, from other laws that reference it.
These firms already pay below union scale; repeal would erase the prevailing-wage requirement that raises their bids on federal work, giving them a direct cost advantage on public contracts.
